```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center", out.width = "85%")
ROOT <- normalizePath(if (file.exists("DSC536_Project.Rproj")) "." else "..")
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = ROOT)
library(jsonlite)
kable <- knitr::kable
OUT <- file.path(ROOT, "regression", "output")
LLM <- file.path(ROOT, "data", "llm")
```

This document contains the code and a short explanation of every step of the regression part of the
project. It runs offline from the files saved in the repository. The only step that needs the internet
(asking the LLM for predictions) is shown but not re-run; its outputs are saved in `data/llm/`.

**Question.** How is weekly AI use (`ai_hours_per_week`) related to students' critical-thinking score
(0-100) and CGPA (0-4), and does an LLM-based prior, built as in O'Hagan & Ročková (2025), improve the
inference when only a few labelled students are available?

# Data

```{r data}
data_raw <- read.csv(file.path(ROOT, "data", "campus_ai_pulse_2026.csv"), stringsAsFactors = TRUE)
dim(data_raw)

# columns removed before modelling (same as the first draft, bapr2.R): the ID and variables that
# are other outcomes or derived scores rather than predictors
DROP_COLS <- c("uses_ai", "paid_ai_subscription", "prompt_skill_level", "time_saved_pct",
               "ai_dependency_score", "ai_dependency_level", "integrity_concern_level",
               "flagged_by_ai_detector", "would_recommend_ai")
data <- data_raw[, setdiff(names(data_raw), DROP_COLS)]
kable(data.frame(column = names(data_raw),
                 type = sapply(data_raw, function(v) class(v)[1]),
                 used = ifelse(names(data_raw) %in% names(data) & names(data_raw) != "student_id",
                               "yes", "no"), row.names = NULL))
```

```{r outcomes, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 3.2}
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
for (v in c("critical_thinking_score", "cgpa", "ai_hours_per_week"))
  hist(data[[v]], breaks = 40, main = v, xlab = v, col = "grey80")
```

## Data checks

`data_check.R` checks types, missing values, duplicates, impossible values, distributions, rare levels,
leakage, collinearity and the OLS fit. The summary table:

```{r data-check}
Sys.setenv(CHECK_OUT_DIR = file.path(OUT, "data_check"))
invisible(capture.output(source(file.path(ROOT, "regression", "data_check.R"), local = new.env())))
chk <- read.csv(file.path(OUT, "data_check", "summary_checks.csv"))
kable(chk[!grepl("^LLM|Split|AI rows|NA in LLM", chk$check), c("check", "result", "problem")])
```

Main points: the data are clean (no missing values, duplicates or impossible values, no leakage), but
`cgpa` is almost perfectly normal and capped at 4, which suggests the dataset is **simulated**, and the
signal is weak. `primary_use_case = "No AI use"` is the same 148 rows as `primary_ai_tool = "No AI tool"`,
so it is dropped from the "all covariates" models.

## The target: OLS on all 1200 students

```{r ols-truth}
fit_s <- lm(critical_thinking_score ~ ai_hours_per_week, data = data)
fit_g <- lm(cgpa ~ ai_hours_per_week, data = data)
kable(rbind(score = c(coef(fit_s)[2], confint(fit_s)[2, ], R2 = summary(fit_s)$r.squared),
            cgpa  = c(coef(fit_g)[2], confint(fit_g)[2, ], R2 = summary(fit_g)$r.squared)),
      digits = 4, col.names = c("beta(ai_hours)", "2.5%", "97.5%", "R2"))
```

One more hour of AI use per week goes with about 0.3 points lower critical-thinking score, and a very
small positive change in CGPA. Both effects explain only 1-2% of the variance.

# LLM predictions (the AI prior)

`llm_prior_labels.R` splits the students with a fixed seed into **300 labelled** ("known") rows and
**900 AI rows** whose outcomes are hidden. For every AI row it asks an LLM (`gpt-oss-20b` on Groq) for a
probability distribution over 8 CGPA bins and 10 score bins, given the student's features only.
This needs an API key, so it is not re-run here:

```{r llm-run, eval = FALSE}
# needs GROQ_API_KEY in ~/.Renviron; resumes from the cache if interrupted
source("regression/llm_prior_labels.R")
```

One saved answer (students are matched back by their id, not by position):

```{r llm-example}
split <- readRDS(file.path(LLM, "llm_split_v2.rds"))
resp  <- readRDS(file.path(LLM, "llm_responses_v2.rds"))
cat(substr(resp[[1]]$text, 1, 400), "...\n")
c(known = length(split$known_ids), ai = length(split$ai_ids))
```

## How good are the LLM predictions?

The true outcomes of the AI rows are used **only** here, to evaluate the LLM.

```{r llm-quality, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4}
probs <- readRDS(file.path(LLM, "llm_probs_v2.rds"))
truth <- data[match(probs$student_id, data$student_id), ]
llm_quality <- function(pr, tr) data.frame(
  outcome   = c("critical_thinking_score", "cgpa"),
  mean_llm  = c(mean(pr$exp_score), mean(pr$exp_cgpa)),
  mean_true = c(mean(tr$critical_thinking_score), mean(tr$cgpa)),
  cor       = c(cor(pr$exp_score, tr$critical_thinking_score), cor(pr$exp_cgpa, tr$cgpa)),
  slope_llm  = c(coef(lm(pr$exp_score ~ tr$ai_hours_per_week))[2], coef(lm(pr$exp_cgpa ~ tr$ai_hours_per_week))[2]),
  slope_true = c(coef(lm(tr$critical_thinking_score ~ tr$ai_hours_per_week))[2], coef(lm(tr$cgpa ~ tr$ai_hours_per_week))[2]))
kable(llm_quality(probs, truth), digits = 3)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(truth$critical_thinking_score, probs$exp_score, pch = 16, col = "#0000ff40",
     xlab = "true score", ylab = "LLM expected score", main = "critical thinking"); abline(0, 1, col = 2)
plot(truth$cgpa, probs$exp_cgpa, pch = 16, col = "#0000ff40",
     xlab = "true CGPA", ylab = "LLM expected CGPA", main = "CGPA"); abline(0, 1, col = 2)
```

The LLM is too optimistic and its predictions are essentially uncorrelated with the truth. Most
importantly, its implied effect of AI hours on critical thinking has the **opposite sign** to the data.

# Method

**Setting.** We have $n$ labelled students $(Y_i, X_i)$ and $m$ unlabelled students $X^*_j$ for which
the LLM gives a predictive distribution $f_{AI}(Y \mid X^*_j)$. The parameter of interest is the
regression coefficient of `ai_hours_per_week`, defined as the minimiser of the squared-error loss.

**AI prior (paper, Section 3.2).** A Dirichlet process prior $F \sim DP(\alpha, F_{AI})$ on the
data-generating distribution, whose base measure $F_{AI}$ is "features of the unlabelled students,
labels drawn from the LLM". The concentration $\alpha$ is the prior strength: the prior is worth
$\alpha$ data points. $\alpha = 0$ uses only the real data; $\alpha = m$ treats every AI row like a
real one (what the first draft did).

**Posterior bootstrap (paper, Algorithm 1).** For $t = 1, \dots, B$: draw fake rows from $F_{AI}$,
draw weights $(w_{1:n}, w^*_{1:m}) \sim \text{Dir}(1, \dots, 1, \alpha/m, \dots, \alpha/m)$, and compute
the weighted least-squares fit. The $B$ fitted coefficients are draws from the posterior.

A minimal version for `score ~ ai_hours` with the 300 known students:

```{r pb-demo, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
set.seed(30175)
X  <- cbind(1, data$ai_hours_per_week); y <- data$critical_thinking_score
kn <- match(split$known_ids, data$student_id)            # 300 labelled rows
ai <- match(split$ai_ids, data$student_id)               # 900 AI rows
P  <- as.matrix(probs[paste0("p_score_", 1:10)])         # LLM distribution per AI row
lo <- seq(0, 90, 10)

posterior_bootstrap <- function(alpha, B = 1000, m = length(ai)) {
  replicate(B, {
    w  <- rgamma(length(kn), 1)                          # Dirichlet(1,...,1) for real rows
    s  <- sample(length(ai), m, replace = TRUE)          # X* from the unlabelled students
    ys <- lo[apply(P[s, ], 1, function(p) sample(10, 1, prob = p))] + runif(m, 0, 10)  # Y* ~ LLM
    ws <- if (alpha > 0) rgamma(m, alpha / m) else rep(0, m)                           # Dir(alpha/m)
    Xa <- rbind(X[kn, ], X[ai[s], ]); ya <- c(y[kn], ys); wa <- c(w, ws)
    solve(crossprod(Xa, Xa * wa), crossprod(Xa, ya * wa))[2]
  })
}
alphas <- c(0, 30, 300, 900)
draws  <- lapply(alphas, posterior_bootstrap)
plot(NA, xlim = range(unlist(draws)), ylim = c(0, 9), xlab = "beta(ai_hours) on critical thinking",
     ylab = "posterior density", main = "Posterior bootstrap, n = 300 known students")
for (k in seq_along(alphas)) lines(density(draws[[k]]), col = k, lwd = 2)
abline(v = coef(fit_s)[2], lty = 2)
legend("topright", c(paste("alpha =", alphas), "OLS on all 1200"), col = c(seq_along(alphas), 1),
       lty = c(rep(1, length(alphas)), 2), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

As $\alpha$ grows, the posterior moves from the real-data estimate towards the LLM's (wrong) positive
effect. The whole question is therefore **how to choose $\alpha$**.

**Choosing $\alpha$ (paper, Section 4.1).**

* *Out-of-sample:* 10-fold cross-validated log predictive density on the known rows ("CV").
* *Coverage calibration (Section 4.1.1):* bootstrap the known rows, treat the known-data estimate as
  the truth of the bootstrap world, and take the **largest** $\alpha$ whose 90% intervals still cover it
  at least 90% of the time ("cal"). Inside this loop the posterior-bootstrap interval is replaced by its
  normal approximation from the paper's Theorem 1, which is much faster.

**Comparison prior.** We also fit the "power" (catalytic) AI prior of the paper's Section 2.1, which
raises the AI-row likelihood to the power $\alpha/m$. With a normal linear model this is conjugate
(closed form), and we average the AI log-likelihood over the full LLM distribution instead of using one
sampled label.

The full implementation is `regression_power_prior.R` (see the Appendix). It repeats everything for
both outcomes, with `ai_hours` only and with all covariates, with 300 and 100 known students, on the
saved split and on 100 random splits (600 AI rows each; the truth is the OLS fit on all rows not used
as known rows).

```{r rerun, eval = params$rerun_analysis}
Sys.setenv(LLM_TAG = "v2")
source(file.path(ROOT, "regression", "regression_power_prior.R"), local = new.env())
```

# Results

```{r load-results}
single  <- read.csv(file.path(OUT, "single_split_summary.csv"))
rep_sum <- read.csv(file.path(OUT, "replicates_summary.csv"))
rep_alpha <- read.csv(file.path(OUT, "replicates_by_alpha.csv"))
getv <- function(model, n, setting, col)
  rep_sum[rep_sum$model == model & rep_sum$n_known == n & rep_sum$setting == setting, col]
```

## One split

Posterior mean and 90% interval of the AI-hours coefficient (`a=` gives the chosen $\alpha$):

```{r single-table}
kable(single[, c("model", "n_known", "truth", "known_only", "pooled_w1", "power_cv", "pb_cal")])
```

```{r single-fig, echo = FALSE, out.width = "95%"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(OUT, "beta_ai_vs_alpha_n300.png"), rel_path = FALSE)
```

## 100 random splits

```{r rep-table}
settings <- c(known_only = "real data only (alpha = 0)", pooled_w1 = "1:1 pooling (alpha = m)",
              power_cv = "power prior, alpha by CV", power_cal = "power prior, alpha by calibration",
              pb_cal = "posterior bootstrap, alpha by calibration")
tab <- rep_sum[rep_sum$setting %in% names(settings),
               c("model", "n_known", "setting", "mean_alpha", "bias", "rmse", "coverage", "sign_ok")]
tab$setting <- settings[tab$setting]
kable(tab, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("model", "n known", "method", "mean alpha", "bias", "RMSE", "90% coverage", "correct sign"))
```

```{r rep-figs, echo = FALSE, out.width = "95%"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(OUT, c("calibration_n300.png", "replicates_rmse_by_alpha.png")), rel_path = FALSE)
```

## What the results show

* **1:1 pooling fails.** For critical thinking with 300 known students, the 90% interval covers the
  truth in `r round(100 * getv("score_only", 300, "pooled_w1", "coverage"))`% of splits and the sign is
  correct in `r round(100 * getv("score_only", 300, "pooled_w1", "sign_ok"))`% (real data only:
  `r round(100 * getv("score_only", 300, "known_only", "coverage"))`% and
  `r round(100 * getv("score_only", 300, "known_only", "sign_ok"))`%).
* **Choosing $\alpha$ by CV protects the analysis.** CV gives the AI rows almost no weight (mean
  $\alpha$ = `r round(getv("score_only", 300, "power_cv", "mean_alpha"), 1)` for `score_only`), so the
  results are as good as with real data only, and slightly better in the models with many covariates.
* **Coverage calibration is too permissive with a biased LLM and few labels.** Its bootstrap estimate of
  coverage follows the actual coverage closely on average (figure above), but choosing the *largest*
  acceptable $\alpha$ often overshoots: with 100 known students the coverage drops to
  `r round(100 * getv("score_only", 100, "power_cal", "coverage"))`%.
* **Posterior bootstrap vs power prior.** Both give almost the same estimates; the posterior bootstrap
  gives wider, more honest intervals when the AI weight is large.
* **Where the prior helps.** For CGPA with all covariates the LLM's (near-zero) adjusted effect is close
  to the truth, and the AI rows stabilise the many coefficients (RMSE
  `r signif(getv("cgpa_all", 300, "known_only", "rmse"), 2)` → `r signif(getv("cgpa_all", 300, "pooled_w1", "rmse"), 2)`).

# Sensitivity to the LLM and the prompt

`llm_prior_labels_v3.R` repeats the elicitation in the paper's style: one student per call, a detailed
prompt that explains every feature, temperature 0.7, and a larger model (`gpt-oss-120b`).

```{r v3, results = "asis"}
f_v3   <- file.path(LLM, paste0("llm_probs_", params$llm_tag_extra, ".rds"))
out_v3 <- file.path(ROOT, "regression", paste0("output_", params$llm_tag_extra))
if (!file.exists(f_v3)) {
  cat("*The", params$llm_tag_extra, "run is not finished yet; this section fills in automatically",
      "once `", basename(f_v3), "` exists.*\n")
} else {
  p3 <- readRDS(f_v3); t3 <- data[match(p3$student_id, data$student_id), ]
  q  <- rbind(cbind(run = "v2 (gpt-oss-20b, 15 per call)", llm_quality(probs, truth)),
              cbind(run = paste(params$llm_tag_extra, "(paper style)"), llm_quality(p3, t3)))
  print(kable(q, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE))
  if (file.exists(file.path(out_v3, "replicates_summary.csv"))) {
    r3 <- read.csv(file.path(out_v3, "replicates_summary.csv"))
    r3 <- r3[r3$setting %in% names(settings) & r3$model %in% c("score_only", "cgpa_only"),
             c("model", "n_known", "setting", "mean_alpha", "rmse", "coverage", "sign_ok")]
    r3$setting <- settings[r3$setting]
    cat("\n\n100 random splits with the", params$llm_tag_extra, "labels:\n\n")
    print(kable(r3, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE))
  } else {
    cat("\n\n*Run `Sys.setenv(LLM_TAG = \"", params$llm_tag_extra,
        "\"); source(\"regression/regression_power_prior.R\")` to add the 100-split results.*\n", sep = "")
  }
}
```

# Limitations

* The dataset looks simulated, so the LLM has no real-world knowledge to contribute and the effects
  should not be read as real findings.
* The effects are weak (R² ≈ 1-2%), so the real data alone already give a wide interval.
* The LLM prior is only as good as the LLM and the prompt; Section 5 checks a second model and prompt.
* The posterior is centred at a biased value whenever $\alpha > 0$ and the LLM is biased (paper,
  discussion after Theorem 1); the method does not correct this bias, it only limits its weight.
* We did not implement the paper's comparison with prediction-powered inference (PPI), which needs
  LLM predictions for the labelled rows as well.

# Reproducibility

* `data_check.R`: about 10 s. `regression_power_prior.R`: about 20 min, offline.
* `llm_prior_labels.R` / `llm_prior_labels_v3.R`: need `GROQ_API_KEY`; their outputs are saved in
  `data/llm/`.
* Set `rerun_analysis: true` in the header to recompute the 100-split study while knitting.

```{r session}
sessionInfo()
```
